findings.title: The opening description uses confusing technical language
findings.evidence: “Leverage our multimodal generative narrative engine to synthesise bespoke, heirloom-grade story artefacts from your household's lived-experience corpus.”
findings.why: I do not understand most of that sentence, and phrases such as “generative engine” and “lived-experience corpus” make the service feel more complicated and less trustworthy.

findings.title: Decorative image has no description
findings.evidence: [image (no description) 430x440]
findings.why: A missing alternative description makes the page less accessible, although it does not prevent me from using the site.

findings.title: The most prominent start action does not say whether login is required
findings.evidence: [5] “Proceed →” goes to /create.html, while a separate “Log in” control is in the header.
findings.why: I cannot tell from the homepage whether I should log in first or whether “Proceed” will preserve my work.

findings.title: Email and password fields have no permanent labels
findings.evidence: [5] is described as a 'textbox (no label)' with placeholder 'Email', and [6] is a 'textbox (no label)' with placeholder 'Password'.
findings.why: The placeholders look reasonably clear now, but I would like the wording to remain visible after typing, especially if I become unsure which box is which.

findings.title: Footer links and copyright have very faint contrast
findings.evidence: The footer displays 'Privacy', 'Terms', 'Contact', and '© 2026 StoryHearth Ltd.' in very pale grey against the cream background.
findings.why: I have some difficulty reading small, faint text, and these links help me check privacy, terms, and how to contact the company.

findings.title: Unexplained technical error undermines confidence
findings.evidence: “Error 0x80070057: profile sync incomplete.”
findings.why: I do not know whether my account is incomplete, whether information may be missing, or whether creating a book could go wrong. An unexplained code is not useful guidance.

findings.title: The error gives no clear consequence or recovery route
findings.evidence: The banner contains only “profile sync incomplete” and provides no button or instructions.
findings.why: I cannot tell whether the site is still working, whether the problem matters, or what I should do next.

findings.title: Personal greeting uses the account placeholder rather than my name
findings.evidence: “Welcome back, Demo”
findings.why: It makes the account feel like a demonstration and less personal than a keepsake service should.

findings.title: Footer links have very low contrast
findings.evidence: “Privacy”, “Terms”, “Contact”, and “© 2026 StoryHearth Ltd.” appear in very pale grey.
findings.why: I can barely read these important links, especially the privacy and terms.

findings.title: Footer text has very low contrast
findings.evidence: The footer text “Privacy”, “Terms”, “Contact” and “© 2026 StoryHearth Ltd.” is very pale grey against the near-white background.
findings.why: I can barely read these links, and I may miss the privacy information or contact route.

findings.title: The form does not state that the other person can be the book creator
findings.evidence: “Who else is in the story?” and the examples “e.g. Grandma Rose” appear, but there is no explanation that I may enter my own name.
findings.why: I want our family story to include both Oliver and me, but the wording briefly makes me wonder whether this field is meant only for another family member.

findings.title: Vague label for the object field
findings.evidence: “A special object”
findings.why: I know the blue kite is important, but the wording does not tell me whether the site wants a treasured possession, something central to the event, or merely a decorative detail.

findings.title: Footer links have very faint contrast
findings.evidence: “Privacy”, “Terms”, and “Contact” appear in very pale grey text in the footer
findings.why: I may need to check privacy or contact details, but the faint lettering is difficult for me to read comfortably.

findings.title: Reading-age scale is unexplained jargon
findings.evidence: The labels “Lexile BR–200L,” “Lexile 200L–500L,” “Lexile 500L–800L,” and “Lexile 800L+” appear without a plain-English explanation.
findings.why: I would be wary of choosing the wrong level for Oliver and would have to guess.

findings.title: The selected reading level is not clearly matched to a five-year-old
findings.evidence: “Lexile 200L–500L” is checked, although the intended reader is five years old.
findings.why: I know Oliver’s age, so I expect the site to recommend a suitable level rather than leave me to interpret the scale.

findings.title: My long story description was silently truncated
findings.evidence: The previous field accepted 493 characters but displayed only 200 characters, with the end cut off: “...'d blue shirt. We took the blue kite up to the windy hill beh”.
findings.why: I cannot tell whether the complete family memory was saved. Important details may be lost, and I do not want to discover that only after the book has been generated.

findings.title: The photo upload control lacks a meaningful page label
findings.evidence: [30] file-upload (no label); the only visible wording is the browser control “Choose file”
findings.why: I can infer what it is for from the heading, but “Choose file” alone does not say whose photograph this is or reassure me that the photograph is truly optional.

findings.title: The reason and handling of a child's photo are not explained here
findings.evidence: “Upload a clear photo of your child's face so the illustrations look like them.”
findings.why: I would hesitate to upload a child's photograph without knowing how long it is kept, whether it is used to train anything, who can access it, or whether deleting the book deletes it.

findings.title: Footer text has very low contrast
findings.evidence: The footer items “Privacy”, “Terms”, “Contact” and “© 2026 StoryHearth Ltd.” are pale grey on a cream background
findings.why: I can hardly read the privacy and contact details, which are particularly important when deciding whether to share a child's photograph.

findings.title: The title is misspelled on the cover
findings.evidence: The page heading and cover both read “The Magical Adventrue of Oliver.”
findings.why: A misspelled title on the front of a keepsake for a five-year-old would be embarrassing and would undermine my confidence in the rest of the writing.

findings.title: The selected illustration style appears not to have been used
findings.evidence: I selected “Storybook classic — timeless ink and colour,” but the preview states “Illustration style: Pop-art comic.”
findings.why: I chose a style specifically because I wanted something warm and suitable for a young child, and I cannot tell whether that choice was ignored or changed.

findings.title: Oliver's requested appearance is missing from the cover
findings.evidence: I described Oliver as having “brown curly hair, freckles, and green wellies,” but the cover shows a generic figure without visible freckles, curls, or green wellies.
findings.why: I supplied those details to make the book personal, so I would like to see at least some of them reflected in the illustrations.

findings.title: The next-page control has an ambiguous symbol
findings.evidence: Control [7] is labelled only “›”.
findings.why: The symbol is familiar, but a written label would be more reassuring and accessible.

findings.title: The final sentence is incomplete
findings.evidence: “And from that day on, whenever Oliver looked up at the sky, he would always remember”
findings.why: As a retired teacher, I expect a complete and satisfying ending in a children's book. This sentence leaves the ending unfinished and makes the finished book feel careless.

findings.title: Optional gift wrap is pre-selected
findings.evidence: [6] checkbox "Premium gift wrap" (checked), with "£7.99" shown beneath it
findings.why: I did not ask for gift wrap, and an unexpected £7.99 raises the total without my consent. I want to know the actual basic price before deciding anything.

findings.title: Checkout uses a reservation countdown
findings.evidence: "Your price is reserved for 09:57"
findings.why: A countdown may make me rush into an order, especially when the optional extra and delivery cost need checking carefully.

findings.title: Hardcover price is not broken down clearly enough
findings.evidence: "Hardcover ... £24.99", "Shipping & handling £12.99", and "Total £45.97"
findings.why: I need to know the delivered cost without extras before deciding whether the book is worthwhile, and the large total does not make that clear at a glance.

findings.title: The purpose of the gift-wrap charge is not explained
findings.evidence: The only wording beside the charge is “Premium gift wrap” and “£7.99”.
findings.why: Before deciding whether an extra cost is worthwhile, I need to know what it includes and why it might be worth £7.99.

findings.title: The gift-wrap checkbox is small and visually detached from its label
findings.evidence: [6] is a very small, empty square positioned above and slightly apart from “Premium gift wrap”.
findings.why: The control is difficult to see, and the spacing makes it less obvious that the label and price belong to the checkbox.

findings.title: The meaning of the price-reservation timer is unclear
findings.evidence: The page says “Your price is reserved for 09:39” but does not explain whether this is a price guarantee, a stock hold, or merely a countdown.
findings.why: The wording sounds more consequential than it may be, and I prefer information to be explicit before I make a decision.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The title visibly says “The Magical Adventrue of Oliver.”

findings.title: visual_quality
findings.evidence: The cover is a very sparse flat illustration, and the page labels the style as “Pop-art comic” rather than the requested “Classic” timeless ink-and-colour style.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: The pictured child has a plain round head and brown hair, with no visible freckles, curly hair, or green wellies described in the inputs.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The cover image shows Oliver, a kite, and a hill, but does not show the old Welsh farmhouse clearly as the special family setting.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The page visibly contains the placeholders “{{recipient_name}}” and “{{sender_name}}.”

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The recipient should be Oliver, and the sender should be Grandma Maggie, but neither name is shown.

findings.title: emotional_resonance
findings.evidence: An unfinished template makes the book feel generated rather than personally made.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The phrase “in the windy hill” is grammatically awkward; “on the windy hill” would be natural.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The input memory says that “my father made me a kite,” but the story only says “Grandpa's old blue shirt” and does not identify the maker as Grandma Maggie's father.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The picture shows the hill, farmhouse, Oliver, and kite, but the text's special detail that the kite was made from Grandpa's old blue shirt is not shown.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: The sentence uses “ephemeral,” “crepuscular,” “engendered,” “inexplicable melancholy,” “juxtaposing,” and “existential trepidation.” The measurement also gives a Flesch-Kincaid grade of 8.5 for a requested reading age of 5.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The prose is technically elaborate but unnecessarily difficult, and the tool flags “crepuscular” as a possible non-word or typo.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The picture shows an evening sky, but not the “ephemeral luminescence” or any clear kite-related event.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text says rain, grey drops, puddles, a hood, and running for shelter, while I5 shows sunshine, no rain, and no puddles.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: “Olive pulled up his hood” uses the wrong name; the character is Oliver.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The story changes the warm shared kite-flying memory into an unrequested rainstorm, with no indication that this is the original family event.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: “Uncle Bartholomew” is an invented character and was not among the supplied family details.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: The text says “she followed him,” although Oliver was specified as “he / him” and is referred to as Oliver immediately beforehand.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The picture shows Uncle Bartholomew with Oliver, but Oliver is standing still rather than following him along the winding path.

findings.title: character_consistency
findings.evidence: The tall figure is labelled Uncle Bartholomew but is not described in the inputs; Oliver's appearance remains inconsistent with the supplied curly hair and freckles.

findings.title: age_fit
findings.evidence: The text says “the shadows grew teeth” and that Oliver “trembled in the dark,” creating an unnecessary frightening threat for a five-year-old.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The dark woods, threatening shadows, and red balloon were not part of the supplied memory and displace the central kite-flying story.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The picture shows a red balloon and a dark night, but the trees do not have teeth and the image does not clearly show whispering shadows.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: The sentence “Once upon a time, in the windy hill behind the old farmhouse in Wales, there lived a curious child named Oliver” repeats the opening of Page 1 and interrupts the progression.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: Oliver “skipped all the way home” even though the requested memory was about flying the kite with Grandma Maggie on the same hill.

findings.title: text_image_fit
findings.evidence: The text says Oliver skipped home, but the picture shows him standing still on the hill.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: The previous page says Oliver is in the dark woods, while this page begins with the original opening and does not explain how he returned to the hill or farmhouse.

findings.title: language
findings.evidence: The sentence ends as “he would always remember” without a completion, and “The End” appears twice.

findings.title: coherence
findings.evidence: The closing does not complete the thought and does not say what Oliver remembers or how the family memory is passed on.

findings.title: fidelity
findings.evidence: The final reflection should connect the kite to Oliver and Grandma Maggie, but neither the kite nor Grandma Maggie appears in the text or picture.

findings.title: emotional_resonance
findings.evidence: The unfinished final sentence makes the book feel unfinished and unsuitable to give as a treasured family keepsake.
